title: The cost of having enough.
name: Demand & Inventory Lab
summary: A replenishment simulator that makes the trade-off between stockouts, service and inventory cost visible.
question: Does a better demand forecast actually produce a better inventory decision?
problem: Stockouts lose sales, but excess stock ties up cash. A forecast accuracy score alone does not tell an operations team which replenishment policy to use.
approach: Generate 224 days of transparent synthetic demand for 12 SKUs, including weekly patterns, intermittent demand and a temporary promotion.
Use the first 84 days as warm-up. Compare rolling-mean and weekday-aware forecasts on the next 140 days, using only observations available at each decision.
Simulate daily receipts, sales, lost demand and new orders across three lead times and four safety buffers. Reconcile every unit of stock.
finding: At a seven-day lead time and a 1.645 buffer, the seasonal policy has lower forecast error, but holds more inventory. Both achieve about 99.6% unit fill. The decision depends on the service and working-capital trade-off, not forecast accuracy alone.
validation: Tests confirm that changing future demand cannot change earlier decisions.
Opening stock + receipts − sales equals closing stock for every simulated day.
Orders arrive at the configured lead time; demand always equals fulfilled units plus lost units.
limitations: Synthetic demand is fully observed, including lost demand. Real sales data may be censored by stockouts. Lead times and unit economics are fixed, replenishment capacity is unlimited, and the safety multiplier is a heuristic rather than a guaranteed service level. Holding cost plus lost margin is an illustrative decision cost, not a complete profit model. The test set describes trade-offs; it does not establish a universally optimal policy.

title: Revenue, with the receipts.
name: Subscription Revenue Forensics
summary: An auditable SQL model that explains recurring revenue through new business, expansion, churn and reactivation.
question: What changed in recurring revenue—and can every dollar be explained?
problem: A single recurring-revenue total can hide churn, contraction and reactivation. Duplicate events can also inflate reporting unless the transformation is auditable.
approach: Validate 985 synthetic contract-change events and isolate 22 exceptions, including duplicate IDs, negative amounts and missing customer IDs.
Build a customer-month spine in SQLite. Carry the latest contracted amount forward and use window functions to classify each movement.
Reconcile opening MRR plus new business, reactivation and expansion, less contraction and churn, to closing MRR. Track customer retention by original acquisition cohort.
finding: The September 2026 example closes at $69,891 in monthly recurring revenue. Its $2,703 net increase includes reactivation and expansion as well as churn and contraction. All 42 month-by-segment bridges reconcile to the cent.
validation: Fixtures distinguish first-time acquisition from reactivation after churn.
Duplicate events cannot increase MRR; a month without an event carries the existing contract forward.
All monetary transformations use integer cents and assert a zero reconciliation residual.
limitations: This model represents end-of-month contracted MRR, not cash collections or accounting revenue recognition. It assumes one currency, a stable customer segment and full-month effective changes. It excludes proration, discounts, foreign exchange and multi-contract accounts. Cohort retention can rise after reactivation; it is active-customer retention, not continuous survival.

title: A lift is only the beginning.
name: Experiment Decision Studio
summary: A decision scorecard that checks uncertainty, sample allocation and error-rate guardrails before calling an A/B test a win.
question: Is an apparent conversion improvement reliable enough—and safe enough—to ship?
problem: A positive lift can be small, uncertain or caused by broken telemetry. A conversion gain can also come with unacceptable product errors.
approach: Analyze one user-level observation per variant in a fixed-horizon synthetic experiment, with conversion as the primary metric and product errors as a guardrail.
Check expected 50/50 allocation with a chi-square sample-ratio test before interpreting the treatment effect.
Use a two-sided 95% interval for the conversion difference and a one-sided 95% upper bound for error-rate harm. Compare them with explicit practical thresholds.
finding: In the balanced example, conversion increases by 0.85 percentage points, but the interval’s lower bound does not establish the default 0.20-point practical lift. A separate scenario is stopped for product errors, and another is blocked for missing treatment telemetry.
validation: A balanced allocation returns an SRM p-value of 1; intentional treatment-data loss fails the allocation gate.
Interval calculations are checked against the two-proportion formula and reverse correctly when groups are swapped.
Allocation failures and guardrail regressions override a positive primary metric.
limitations: These are synthetic, independent-user, fixed-horizon examples. Normal approximations require adequate successes and failures, which the code checks. Threshold changes in this demo are sensitivity analysis; a real experiment should specify decision rules before launch. Device slices are descriptive and have no multiple-comparison-adjusted inference. This is not a sequential-testing engine.

title: From survey data to decisions.
name: Survey Operations Dashboard
summary: A clear view of response quality, completion and satisfaction across six markets, with definitions and an audit trail.
question: Which markets need attention, and can the underlying responses be trusted?
problem: Headline satisfaction scores need context: completion, channel mix, sample sizes and response quality can change the interpretation.
approach: Validate synthetic survey exports with an explicit rejection audit.
Recalculate metrics from the underlying rows for each market, channel and period filter.
Show response trends, ranked market metrics, quality checks and precise denominator definitions.
finding: The full demonstration contains 7,200 usable responses, 87.7% completion and 76.3% customer satisfaction. The market and channel filters expose the sample behind each headline.
validation: Dashboard totals reconcile to the Python pipeline’s exported rows.
Incomplete responses are excluded from the satisfaction and duration denominators.
limitations: All responses and market results are synthetic. This is an interactive web BI demonstration, not a Power BI report or a representation of a former employer’s data.

title: One command. Trusted data.
name: Python Data Quality Automation
summary: A small, inspectable pipeline that validates, deduplicates and transforms survey exports into reporting-ready data.
question: How can a repetitive data-cleaning task become a reproducible, auditable process?
problem: Manual cleaning makes it easy to lose rejected rows, change metric definitions or overwrite the original export.
approach: Check the input schema and preserve a source checksum.
Keep the first valid response ID and isolate failed records with a reason.
Export cleaned data, market summaries, dashboard JSON and a quality report in one run.
finding: The reproducible sample run transforms 7,300 input rows into 7,200 validated rows and 100 isolated exceptions. A 38-second captioned walkthrough follows the actual script output.
validation: Six focused tests cover deduplication, KPI denominators, invalid inputs and source preservation.
Clean rows plus rejected rows equal the input count.
limitations: This demonstration uses generated survey data. The video is a paced walkthrough of actual script output, not a live execution recording or a measured production time-saving claim.
